newsitem.title: USA: Alleged Haitian drugs kingpin still in Honduras.
newsitem.headline: Alleged Haitian drugs kingpin still in Honduras.

text.p: Exiled Haitian strongman and alleged drug trafficker Joseph Michel Francois will remain in Honduras at least until Friday as he fights efforts to extradite him to Miami, U.S. officials said on Tuesday.

Francois, arrested by Honduran police and U.S. anti-narcotics agents in a remote part of the Central American country last Friday, was due to appear before a judge in Tegucigalpa on Tuesday, his lawyer in Miami said.
"Whether that will end today I do not know. We're waiting to see what happens down there," attorney Frank Rubino told Reuters.

But the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration said they no longer expected his imminent removal from Honduras to a Miami jail. "We're not anticipating getting him until at least Friday. We won't know until then," DEA spokeswoman Pam Brown said.

U.S. authorities had hoped to whisk Francois, police chief of Port-au-Prince under Haiti's 1991-94 military government, to Miami and into a courthouse last week but their efforts seem to have been frustrated by legal procedures in Honduras.

"I thought all the paperwork had been done and the judge just needed to stamp it," Wilfredo Fernandez, spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office, said. "If he's fighting extradition then Friday might be to early to expect. It could take months -- I don't know how Honduras treats extradition cases."

U.S. drug fighters believe they have caught a man who played a key role in flooding the United States with more than 33 tonnes of cocaine and heroin in the past several years. According to the indictment, Francois turned Haiti into a vast staging point for drugs through his control of the security apparatus.
He had a private landing strip built and put cronies in charge of the airport and seaports in return for millions of dollars in payoffs from Colombian cartels, the indictment said.
Francois protested his innocence at a news conference in a Tegucigalpa jail on Monday. "How many times do I have to say I know nothing about drugs," he said.

He said Washington had targeted him in revenge for his refusal to leave Haiti and hand power back to elected President Jean-Bertrand Aristide. Francois was believed to have been the mastermind behind the 1991 military coup that toppled Aristide and during his tenure as police chief he ran a security apparatus that viciously repressed any opposition.

He fled to the Dominican Republic in 1994 after U.S. troops invaded Haiti to restore Aristide to power. He was given asylum in Honduras a year ago when Dominican authorities arrested him on charges of plotting to overthrow the Haitian government again.

Rubino, who defended former Panamanian strongman Gen. Manuel Noriega in his 1992 drugs trial in Miami, said he had been asked by friends of Francois to represent him. Noriega was convicted and is serving a 40-year prison term.
"We haven't got together to discuss the case. I haven't met the gentleman yet," Rubino said. "But he requested me. I've represented a lot of generals."
